header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Lucas Park (Redwood SE), Riya Patel (Kyros - Head of ML), Tom Nguyen (Kyros - Eng Manager), Sara Lee (Kyros - Security)
summary: Discovery call to understand Kyros Labs' current usage of OpenAI for production LLM features, evaluate Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, and scope a pilot. Key concerns: latency, cost, eval parity with OpenAI, compatibility with vLLM/TGI stack, security (SOC2/SSO/KMS) and audit logs.
topics: Model compatibility and eval parity (OpenAI vs local runtimes)
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment considerations
Security/compliance questions (SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs)
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Lucas is my SE.
[00:06] Riya Patel: Hi Maya, Lucas, thanks. I'm Riya, head of ML at Kyros. Tom and Sara are on as well.
[00:12] Tom Nguyen: Hey all.
[00:14] Sara Lee: Hi.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda: 1) understand your current stack and telemetry, 2) what pain you're seeing with OpenAI, 3) go over Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private, and 4) next steps for a pilot. Does that sound right?
[00:28] Riya Patel: Yep that works.
[00:30] Lucas Park: Great, can I ask first about traffic patterns? average qps, burstiness?
[00:36] Tom Nguyen: Sure. We're doing roughly 20 qps average across our chat assistant API, spikes up to 120 qps for some enterprise customers during batch runs. Latency matters for real-time features; P50 around 300-400ms currently but P95 can spike to 1.2s with OpenAI depending on prompt length.
[00:52] Lucas Park: Helpful. And what's your cost profile look like? tokens/month?
[00:56] Riya Patel: We're around 4B tokens/month, cost is getting material. We're also running internal evals to make sure outputs align with our safety filters.
[01:06] Maya Chen: Okay, so big reasons to consider migration are cost and P95 latency predictability?
[01:11] Riya Patel: Exactly. Also data residency and audit requirements for one of our bigger customers.
[01:16] Sara Lee: And just to flag security: need SOC 2, SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS integration; if we go private we need customer-managed keys and private networking.
[01:27] Maya Chen: Totally understood. Lucas, do you want to cover how Redwood can map to these needs?
[01:32] Lucas Park: Sure. High level: Hosted is the fastest to get started — our API, same as you use now, with model catalog and streaming. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools so throughput and latency are predictable, plus data isolation. Private adds the VPC or on-prem options with customer KMS. For your qps and spikes, Dedicated with burst capacity is a common fit.
[01:52] Tom Nguyen: Can dedicated actually hit P95 of <500ms for our 1k token prompts?
[01:57] Lucas Park: It depends on model choice and batching profile, but with model variants we've seen P95 down to ~300-500ms for 1k token-ish workloads on A100/H100 pools with optimized kernels and KV cache warm. We need to run your prompt-set to confirm.
[02:12] Riya Patel: We run a mix: short instructions and longer context retrieval. Compatibility's a question — we're prototyping with vLLM and TGI locally for cost reasons. How compatible is Redwood with those runtimes and with OpenAI evals?
[02:26] Lucas Park: Two parts: model compatibility and eval parity. For model compatibility, Redwood's serving runtime supports the common model formats and tokenizer behaviors; we onboard open models and also offer compatibility layers for OpenAI-style APIs. For eval parity, we run eval harnesses during onboarding to check generation distribution, tokenization differences, and metric drift. We also do sampling/regeneration to compare outputs.
[02:46] Sarah (sic) Lee: (laugh) Sara. Tokenization differences worry us — we had subtle changes moving from OpenAI to a local Llama variant that changed classification thresholds.
[02:52] Lucas Park: That's a common issue. We usually map tokenizer normalization and run side-by-side diffs on sample prompts. Sometimes we recommend light prompt engineering or a small calibration layer on your side.
[03:03] Riya Patel: On the local stack: If we bring vLLM/TGI models to Redwood Dedicated, is there any work to recompile or change configs?
[03:11] Lucas Park: Not usually. Redwood supports models in standard formats and we optimize kernels at runtime; if you're using vLLM configs, we can translate common flags vs our runtime tuning. In some cases quantization profiles differ, which can affect perf and quality; we'll surface those tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[03:27] Tom Nguyen: How about throughput cost comparisons? We currently pay per-token to OpenAI and we're trying to model dedicated hourly GPU cost + utilization.
[03:35] Maya Chen: We can share a cost model spreadsheet. For your 4B tokens/month, Dedicated with 2-3 reserved nodes plus burst is often cheaper beyond a threshold. It depends on utilization and model size. We'll attach a sample excel.
[03:49] Riya Patel: Another thing: eval parity. Our safety/regression monitoring needs identical behavior across training/validation and production. If outputs drift after migration we need quick rollbacks.
[03:58] Lucas Park: We support pinned model versions, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback to hosted variants. Also Redwood Optimize gives you regression alerts tied to prompt sets and eval metrics. For safety, we recommend running a shadow test — route x% of traffic to the Dedicated instance and compare flags.
[04:16] Sara Lee: Audit logs and access controls — we need per-request logs, redaction, and RBAC with SSO. Can Redwood export to our SIEM?
[04:23] Lucas Park: Yes. Audit logs can ship to your S3 or to SIEM via connectors; RBAC integrates with SAML/SSO and we can do token-level metadata for tracing. For private deployments you can use customer KMS/HSM.
[04:36] Tom Nguyen: If we want to keep some workloads on OpenAI for edge cases, does Redwood support hybrid routing?
[04:41] Maya Chen: Absolutely. Smart routing can send requests by latency/cost policy, region, or model and fallback to hosted OpenAI-compatible variants if Dedicated is saturated.
[04:50] Riya Patel: Okay that sounds promising. For the pilot, we'd want a short benchmark with our prompts, and ideally test both vLLM/TGI local variants and Redwood-optimized variants so we can compare.
[05:00] Lucas Park: That's exactly what we usually do: 48-hour benchmark using your prompt sets, sample traffic shape, measure latency, cost, and eval metrics. We'll instrument token-level cost and P95/P99 latency.
[05:09] Riya Patel: What about deterministic outputs for eval? We use temperature=0 for a lot of tests. Any differences?
[05:14] Lucas Park: Determinism is influenced by seed and sampling implementation. We attempt to match OpenAI's sampling as closely as possible; part of the benchmark is to surface any distributional offsets. If needed we can run nucleus top-p and top-k tuning to match.
[05:28] Tom Nguyen: On the security side, timeline: our procurement needs a SOC2 report and data processing agreement. Can you share those?
[05:33] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll send SOC2 + SOC2 type II report and our standard DPA. For Dedicated/Private we also have architecture docs.
[05:41] Sara Lee: If we go private, do you support on-prem air-gapped installs?
[05:46] Lucas Park: Yes, we have an on-prem package that customers use for regulated workloads; it requires an early integration with our engineering team. It supports customer KMS and local logging.
[05:56] Riya Patel: Regulatory note: some customers require EU-only data residency. Do you support region pinning?
[06:02] Maya Chen: Yes, region pinning is supported for Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted can be regionally constrained depending on plan.
[06:09] Tom Nguyen: Quick Q: for quantized models — if we go 4-bit quantization to save cost, is there a large quality drop for our classification tasks?
[06:17] Lucas Park: It varies by model and task. For many classification tasks, 4-bit quantization with the right calibration gives negligible impact; for generative creative tasks you might see more regressions. We'll include quantization profiles in the benchmark and recommend fallback options.
[06:32] Riya Patel: Good. Another practical — are there SDK changes? We call OpenAI endpoints in production. How much migration work?
[06:38] Maya Chen: Minimal. Redwood's API is OpenAI-compatible for most common calls; we have SDKs and migration guides. For advanced features like streaming or tool calls, we have parity docs and examples.
[06:50] Tom Nguyen: About observability: we currently instrument token-level metrics in our backend. Can we get the same from Redwood and correlate traces?
[06:57] Lucas Park: Yes, we provide token-level cost breakdowns, latency per-step, and tracing hooks you can send to your APM. We also export per-route metrics to Prometheus/Datadog.
[07:08] Riya Patel: Okay good. On the business side, what's a typical pilot commitment?
[07:13] Maya Chen: Usually a 30- to 90-day pilot with a few reserved nodes for Dedicated benchmarks. We can do a usage-based pilot too if you want less upfront. For procurement, pilots often convert to reserved capacity once metrics look good.
[07:25] Tom Nguyen: We have a budget approval window in mid-April — would that timeline work?
[07:29] Maya Chen: Absolutely. If we start the benchmark early March we can have results for your April review.
[07:35] Riya Patel: One more technical: our stack uses retrieval-augmented generation with a vector DB. How do you handle long context and KV cache?
[07:44] Lucas Park: We have built-in KV cache management and prefix caching so when you have repeated contexts we keep KV cache warm. For RAG scenarios, we recommend serving the retrieval results as short contexts and leverage batching; we can show best practices in the benchmark.
[07:59] Sara Lee: Do you support customer-side PII redaction or redaction hooks?
[08:04] Lucas Park: Yes, you can plug in redaction pre- or post-processing. For Private deployments you can run the redactor locally. Hosted options include inline redaction patterns and configurable redaction rules.
[08:17] Riya Patel: Regarding model updates, how are rollouts handled? We don't want silent quality regressions when a model gets patched.
[08:24] Lucas Park: We have rollouts with canary percent, A/B tests, and automatic rollback based on eval regression thresholds. Redwood Optimize monitors prompt-set metrics and can trigger alerts.
[08:36] Tom Nguyen: Can we get an example of the benchmark report?
[08:39] Maya Chen: We'll share a sample with latency, cost, token distributions, and eval metrics.
[08:44] Riya Patel: Great. Any red flags we should know about?
[08:47] Lucas Park: The biggest risk is distributional drift due to tokenizer or model variant differences. We mitigate that with calibration, evals, and canarying. Another is procurement time — enterprise contracts can add time but pilots run parallel.
[09:01] Tom Nguyen: If we wanted to test our vLLM/TGI local recipes on Redwood, can we bring custom kernels or will Redwood recompile?
[09:09] Lucas Park: You can bring your model weights and common config. We handle kernel selection in our runtime — we don't allow arbitrary kernel injection in hosted Dedicated for stability, but with Private or on-prem we can collaborate deeper. For the pilot we'll test your TGI/vLLM outputs and map config differences.
[09:29] Riya Patel: Okay, that makes sense. Pricing: is there a break-even token volume you typically see moving from hosted OpenAI to Dedicated?
[09:36] Maya Chen: It depends on model size and utilization, but often beyond ~1-2B tokens/month Dedicated becomes economical if you can achieve >50% utilization. We'll run your numbers.
[09:47] Sara Lee: For compliance: do you provide evidence for data deletion requests and data lifecycle?
[09:52] Lucas Park: Yes, we support deletion APIs, retention policies, and audit trails for data access, especially in Dedicated/Private. We'll include retention configurations in the security docs.
[10:06] Riya Patel: Sounds good. Let's talk concrete next steps.
[10:09] Maya Chen: Proposed next steps: 1) we'll send pricing + sample contract, 2) Lucas will send benchmark plan and script, 3) Kyros provides prompt sets and some sample traffic, 4) schedule follow-up in about a week for kickoff.
[10:23] Tom Nguyen: Works for us.
[10:25] Sara Lee: Agreed.
[10:27] Riya Patel: One last small ask: can Redwood run an A/B on a few safety-sensitive prompts to compare flag rates?
[10:33] Lucas Park: Yep, we can include safety flag comparison in the benchmark.
[10:37] Maya Chen: Great — we'll follow up with an email summarizing action items. Thanks all for your time.
[10:42] Riya Patel: Thanks.
[10:43] Tom Nguyen: Thanks, bye.
[10:44] Sara Lee: Bye.
[10:45] Maya Chen: End call.

Notes: transcription has occasional mis-hearings and a few speaker label slips (typical automated output).
